extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: MPEP guidance for examining pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 issues including on-sale/public-use, experimental-use doctrines, abandonment (102(c)), foreign-patent bars (102(d)), and certain 102(e) prior-art date issues. Focus is on objective indicia, examiner evaluation steps, and statutory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective intent manifested by objective evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of commercial activity which constitutes 'on sale' status depends upon the circumstances of the activity, the basic indicator being the subjective intent of the inventor as manifested through objective evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should evaluate objective indicia (contracts, documents, conduct) to infer inventor intent; subjective, secretly held intent to experiment is unavailing without objective support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of contemporaneous commercial documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation of various contemporaneous 'commercial' documents, e.g., orders, invoices, receipts, delivery schedules, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such documents are indicia of commercial exploitation and should be used by examiners as evidence of on-sale activity (case citations provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation/distribution of price lists and quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation of price lists and distribution of price quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Price lists and quotations (Akron Brass; Amphenol Corp. examples) are objective evidence indicative of commercial exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display of samples to prospective customers
rubrics_metrics.description: Display of samples to prospective customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Displaying samples (including at trade shows) can indicate commercial exploitation even if no orders were obtained (case law: Cataphote Corp.; Chicopee Mfg.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration of models or prototypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstration of models or prototypes, especially at trade conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations of prototypes/models are strong indicia of on-sale/public-use status; examples include trade convention displays and related case law citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of invention where admission fee is charged
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of an invention where an admission fee is charged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charging an admission fee for use/demonstration is an indicium of commercial exploitation (case examples referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising and publicity as indicia of commercial exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising in publicity releases, brochures, and various periodicals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising and publicity materials are objective evidence of commercial exploitation (In re Theis; Interroyal Corp.; Akron Brass; Tucker Aluminum examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use ends upon actual reduction to practice ('completeness')
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental use 'means perfecting or completing an invention to the point of determining that it will work for its intended purpose.' Therefore, experimental use 'ends with an actual reduction to practice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence shows the inventor considered the invention 'complete,' awaiting approvals (e.g., UL) will not usually overcome that conclusion; see RCA Corp., Interroyal Corp., and Skil Corp. citations. Modifications resulting from experimentation must be features of the claimed invention to be probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposal of prototypes assessed by inventor intent and reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a prototype has been disposed of by an inventor before the critical date, inquiry should focus on the inventor's intent and the reasonableness of the disposal under all circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidental income from a reasonable disposal is not necessarily fatal (In re Dybel), but unrestricted disposal of a 'complete' prototype with experimentation ceased constitutes a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) bar (In re Blaisdell; contra Watson v. Allen). Examiner should examine circumstances carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity for public testing (factor indicative of experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether there was a necessity for public testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider if the invention reasonably required public testing as part of experimental development (listed among the factors from Allen Eng'g Corp. v. Bartell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of control retained by the inventor (factor indicative of experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of control over the experiment retained by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater inventor control during testing supports experimental purpose; lack of control suggests commercial exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the invention (factor indicative of experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some inventions by nature require field testing under real conditions; this affects whether activity is experimental or commercial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of the test period (factor indicative of experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of the test period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, reasonable test periods oriented to experimental objectives favor permissible experimentation; prolonged testing may indicate market testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether payment was made (factor indicative of experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether payment was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment to the inventor/customer during testing is a factor against experimental use and toward commercial exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether there was a secrecy obligation (factor indicative of experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether there was a secrecy obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secrecy obligations (NDA, contractual restrictions) support an experimental purpose by limiting public exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether records of the experiment were kept (factor indicative of experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether records of the experiment were kept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic recordkeeping of tests and results supports bona fide experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who conducted the experiment (factor indicative of experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Who conducted the experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments conducted by the inventor or by persons under inventor's control support experimental use; independent third-party conduct without inventor control undermines it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of commercial exploitation during testing (factor indicative of experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of commercial exploitation during testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant commercial exploitation during testing weighs against an experimental-use finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the invention reasonably requires evaluation under actual conditions of use (factor indicative of experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the invention reasonably requires evaluation under actual conditions of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If realistic field conditions are necessary to evaluate the invention, testing in such conditions may be proper experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether testing was systematically performed (factor indicative of experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether testing was systematically performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic, designed testing protocols are consistent with experimental objectives rather than market testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the inventor continually monitored the invention during testing (factor indicative of experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the inventor continually monitored the invention during testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous inventor supervision and iterative refinement during tests support experimentation; lack of monitoring favors commercial use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of contacts made with potential customers (factor indicative of experimental purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of contacts made with potential customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contacts clearly aimed at marketing/customer acceptance weigh toward commercial exploitation; contacts limited to technical evaluation or recruitment for testing favor experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customer's awareness of purported testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Customer's awareness of the purported testing in the context of a sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customer awareness is a critical attribute: where sales are made in ordinary commercial environments and goods are placed outside inventor's control, the customer must at minimum be made aware of the experimentation (LaBounty; Paragon Podiatry examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of scope and length of experimental activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Once experimental activity is advanced by an applicant, the examiner must determine whether the scope and length of the activity were reasonable in terms of the experimental purpose intended and the nature of the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single factor or combination is necessarily determinative; examiner evaluates overall reasonableness against the claimed purpose and technological context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor must maintain sufficient control during third-party testing
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor must maintain sufficient control over the invention during alleged experimentation by third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control and customer awareness ordinarily must be proven for the experimental-use exception to apply; relinquishment of supervision without restraints may create a statutory bar (Electromotive Div. v. Gen. Motors; In re Blaisdell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental testing is permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing of an invention in the normal context of its technological development is generally within the realm of permitted experimental activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimentation to determine utility (35 U.S.C. 101/112 contexts) and developmental tests to perfect function are permissible absent sales or other evidence of commercial exploitation (examples: chemical composition testing to find utility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Market testing is not permitted (not experimental)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimentation to determine product acceptance, i.e., market testing, is not permitted as experimental activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market testing is typical of a trader's (commercial) activity, not an inventor's experiment. Testing to appease a customer or minor tune-ups requiring only a technician's skills are also not within permitted experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental activity in design applications limited to functional features
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use of an ornamental design directed toward generating consumer interest in aesthetics is not experimental; however, experimentation directed to functional features of a product that also has an ornamental design may negate what otherwise would be considered a public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornamental displays aimed at consumer interest are public use (In re Mann); functional testing of features may be experimental (Tone Brothers v. Sysco example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use doctrine is personal to the inventor (third-party activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use and sales activity may be prior art even if by a party other than an inventor; evidence of experimental activity by another party will not overcome a prima facie case of unpatentability unless the activity was under the supervision and control of the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If tests/experiments are not under inventor's surveillance/control, the inventor generally cannot rely on them to avoid the statutory bar (In re Hamilton; Magnetics, Inc. v. Arnold Engineering).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) requires intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual abandonment under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) requires that the inventor intend to abandon the invention; intent can be implied from conduct but should not be imputed lightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every reasonable doubt resolved in favor of the inventor (Ex parte Dunne; In re Gibbs). Delay alone is not sufficient to infer abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay in reapplying alone does not establish abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay alone is not sufficient to infer the requisite intent to abandon under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts such as drafting and retention of patent applications in inventor's files indicate intent to retain rights (Moore v. United States); however, prolonged inaction may be evidence when coupled with other conduct (Davis Harvester Co. example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure in prior issued patent without claiming is rebuttable
rubrics_metrics.description: Any inference of abandonment of subject matter disclosed but not claimed in a previously issued patent is rebuttable by an application filed at any time before a statutory bar arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) based solely on issuance of a patent that discloses unclaimed subject matter is improper if there is copendency or an intervening application; see In re Gibbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lapse of time bars only in priority contest under 102(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere lapse of time will not bar a patent; the only exception is when there is a priority contest under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) and applicant abandons, suppresses or conceals the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandonment, suppression and concealment are addressed under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) and related MPEP sections (Panduit Corp. v. Dennison Mfg. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) — foreign filing more than 12 months before U.S. effective filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: The foreign application must be filed more than 12 months before the effective U.S. filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of four conditions for a 102(d) statutory bar; note rules on anniversary date falling on weekend/holiday (extension to next business day) and special filing-date treatment (37 CFR provisions) discussed in guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) — same applicant/legal representative/assigns
rubrics_metrics.description: The foreign and United States applications must have been filed by the same applicant or by the same applicant's legal representatives or assigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple inventors may have separate foreign applications; continuation-in-part (CIP) may break priority chains as to particular claim subject matter (Van Langenhoven example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) — the foreign application must have actually issued as a patent before the U.S. filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: The foreign application must have actually issued as a patent or inventor's certificate before the filing in the United States; it need not be published but must have enforceable patent rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be 'patented' an exclusionary right must be awarded (In re Monks); published applications are generally not 'patents' for 102(d) (Ex parte Fujishiro), although allowed applications published for opposition with substantial provisional rights (Auslegeschrift) have been treated as patents for 102(d) (Ex parte Beik). Grant date is the date patent becomes enforceable; secrecy after grant does not negate 102(d) applicability (In re Kathawala).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) — the same invention must be involved
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'same invention' means that the application claims could have been presented in the foreign patent; the foreign specification supporting the U.S. claims can trigger the bar even if claims differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign patent need not have identical claims; if the foreign patent fully discloses the invention and supports U.S. claim subject matter, 102(d) applies (In re Kathawala example). Examiner should assess whether foreign patent supports the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) prior art only when reasonable possibility exists
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should undertake a search for an issued foreign patent for use as pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) prior art only if there is a reasonable possibility that a foreign patent covering the same subject matter has been granted to the same inventive entity before the U.S. effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider typical foreign pendency times, use electronic databases or Scientific and Technical Information Center staff, or require applicant information under 37 CFR 1.105 when reasonable basis exists (see MPEP § 901.06(a) and § 704.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation-in-part (CIP) breaks chain of priority for foreign and U.S. parents
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuation-in-part breaks the chain of priority as to the subject matter added in the CIP; claims not entitled to the parent's filing date have the CIP filing date as effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a foreign application issues before the CIP filing date, it may be used against CIP claims under 102(d)/103 if the added subject matter does not render claims nonobvious over the foreign patent (Van Langenhoven; Ex parte Appeal example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anniversary date extension when falling on weekend/holiday
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. application is filed in time to prevent a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) bar if filed on the 1-year anniversary date of the foreign filing; if that day is a Saturday/Sunday/federal holiday, the year is extended to the following business day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule changes regarding deposit dates (37 CFR) do not affect applicant's concurrent right to defer filing until next business day when last day falls on weekend/holiday; see Ex parte Olah.

rubrics_metrics.name: To be 'patented' an exclusionary right must be awarded
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Patented' means a formal bestowal of patent rights from the sovereign to the applicant (i.e., an exclusionary right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some foreign forms (e.g., Gebrauchsmuster) may be treated as patents for 102(d) depending on their exclusionary effect and legal status in the foreign country; duration and scope distinctions discussed with case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: A published application is not generally a 'patent' for 102(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: A published application must issue into a patent before it can be applied in a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards have held that laid-open or published foreign applications (e.g., Offenlegungsschriften) are not patents for 102(d) (Ex parte Fujishiro; Ex parte Links), except in special procedures where publication for opposition gives substantial provisional enforcement rights (see Ex parte Beik).

rubrics_metrics.name: An allowed application published for opposition can be a 'patent' for 102(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: An examined application which has been allowed and published for opposition has been held to be a 'patent' for 102(d) as of the date published for opposition if substantial provisional enforcement rights arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: German Auslegeschrift practice where provisional rights were comparable to granted patent (Ex parte Beik). Examiner should assess legal effect of foreign publication practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant occurs when patent becomes enforceable (critical date for 102(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical date of a foreign patent as a reference under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) is the date the patent becomes enforceable (issued, sealed or granted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the grant/enforcement date (In re Monks); secrecy periods after grant do not negate the 102(d) reference in most contexts (In re Kathawala; historical examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) — certain U.S. and international applications as prior art as of their U.S. filing dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) allows use of certain international application publications and U.S. patent application publications, and certain U.S. patents as prior art as of their respective U.S. filing dates, including certain international filing dates when conditions met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prior art date of a reference under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) may be the international filing date if the international filing date was on or after November 29, 2000, the international application designated the United States, and was published by WIPO under PCT Article 21(2) in English. Older international applications are subject to pre-AIPA 102(e) rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published SIRs treated as U.S. patents for defensive purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: In accordance with former 35 U.S.C. 157(c), a published SIR (statutory invention registration) will be treated the same as a U.S. patent for all defensive purposes, usable as a reference as of its filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A published SIR is prior art under applicable sections of 35 U.S.C. 102, including pre-AIA 102(e); see MPEP § 1111 for details.
